analysis.one_liner: Raises cleanup bonds and fees for oil and gas drilling on public lands so taxpayers don't pay to plug abandoned wells.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 23–15 and reported it in December 2022, but it never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When an oil or gas company finishes drilling on federal land and walks away, it is supposed to post a bond to cover the cost of restoring the land and plugging the wells. Current bond minimums are decades old and often fall far short of the actual cleanup bill, leaving taxpayers to pay the difference. This bill would raise the minimum bonds to $150,000 per well site and $500,000 per company per state, require bonds to rise with inflation, charge companies annual inspection fees, add a small per-barrel fee to plug abandoned wells, and block bond release until cleanup is verified.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who today can end up footing the bill when a drilling company goes bankrupt or abandons wells without plugging them. Also people who live near federal oil and gas wells, since verified reclamation standards and funded plugging reduce the risk of leaking methane, contaminated water, and scarred land. Deficit-conscious taxpayers benefit from inspection fees and the orphaned-well fee that cover government oversight costs directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and residents near federal oil wells

how_it_helps.text: Requires a bond adequate for the complete and timely reclamation of each lease tract, with minimums of $150,000 per surface-disturbing activity and $500,000 per operator per state, adjusted for inflation at least every three years.
Charges operators annual inspection fees—from $700 to $9,800 depending on well count—sufficient to recover the full cost of federal inspection and enforcement, with inflation adjustments.
Creates a per-barrel fee of at least $0.10 on federal oil and gas production to fund plugging and reclamation of orphaned wells.

Bars release of any bond or financial assurance until reclamation standards are met and inspection fees are paid, and requires uniform interim and final reclamation plans restoring vegetation, hydrology, and habitat before drilling permits are approved.

Authorizes the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to require financial assurances from companies developing minerals under National Wildlife Refuge lands, to cover well plugging, damage response, and restoration.
Prohibits issuing or transferring federal leases to any operator that has failed to comply with reclamation requirements on a prior lease.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal lands, which would face sharply higher bonding costs, new annual inspection fees, and a per-barrel production fee. Some of these costs could be passed through to consumers or to lessors in bidding, and higher compliance costs could push small federal-land operators out of business or off federal leases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal lands

drawbacks.text: Higher bonds, annual fees of up to $9,800 per lease, and a per-barrel charge raise operating costs on federal leases; small independent operators are the least able to absorb them and could exit federal lands or fail, and some cost could reach consumers through energy prices.
The largest bond increases are phased in over three years (25% after one year, 75% after two, 100% after three), so protection against under-bonded wells is limited in the near term.
Requiring a full ecosystem-restoration standard—restoring pre-drilling vegetation, hydrology, and habitat—as a condition of every drilling permit could slow permitting on federal lands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: companies that profit from drilling on public land would pay the real cost of restoring it, instead of leaving the bill to taxpayers when wells are abandoned. The costs are real but narrowly targeted at federal-land operations, and the fee structure is designed to cover the government's own inspection costs rather than grow a bureaucracy. The main honest concern is transition risk for small operators and possible pass-through to energy prices; the bill's phase-in schedule partly addresses this.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee in May 2021 and was reported to the House floor in the final days of the Congress in December 2022, but House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the term ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2021 by Rep. Alan Lowenthal and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
After a subcommittee hearing, the subcommittee was discharged and the full committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 23–15 on May 5, 2021.
The committee reported the bill with an amendment on December 14, 2022 (H. Rept. 117-629) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, which is the list of bills eligible for House floor action.
No floor vote ever occurred; the bill sat on the calendar until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal-land oil and gas operators are better off because the bill never became law: they avoided higher bonding minimums, annual inspection fees, and the per-barrel orphaned-well charge. Taxpayers continue to carry the risk of paying to plug and reclaim wells abandoned without adequate bonds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators avoided the new costs

industries.industry: Oil and gas operators on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would require these companies to post bonds covering the full cost of reclaiming drill sites and plugging idle wells, pay annual inspection fees of $700–$9,800 per lease, and pay a $0.10-per-barrel orphaned-well fee. Their savings from the current low-bond system come directly at taxpayer expense when wells are abandoned.
The per-barrel orphaned-well fee would fund plugging and reclamation work, creating paid cleanup work and reducing the backlog of abandoned federal wells that leak methane and threaten groundwater.

Higher, inflation-adjusted bond minimums and required bond reviews at every lease transfer would expand demand for the surety bonds operators must post. The cost is borne by operators, not the public.
